title: The data center backlash won’t last
subtitle: Data Center opposition will look like cellphone tower opposition in two years.
html:
On the surface the movement against data centers in the United States has never looked more powerful. The industry lost all three local referendums this year. Moratorium bills are sitting in a dozen statehouses and general opposition in polling has gone from 43% to 75% in under a year.

I think November 2026 and its accompanying election will be the apex of this whole movement, and it won’t be a top 5 issue by November 2027. People two years from now will regard being anti-data-center with the same contempt that they reserve for people who believe cell phone and 5G towers are bad. This whole movement will devolve into a shibboleth of online leftism and libertarianism and will be relegated to the dustbin of politics.

Quincy, Washington took 56 data centers and their poverty rate fell from nearly 30% to 6.2%. Meanwhile there is no contaminant, no plume, no poisoned wells waiting to be discovered. There will never be an Erin Brockovich in this fight. A public scandal with no tort at the end is just a fight about politics- a politics that will wither away after the midterm.

Only 8% of the people who oppose data centers say that there’s one near them. 30% of supporters do. 63% of opponents hold a negative view of AI, against 8% of supporters. Pew geolocated the whole country and found that 42% of us live within 5 miles of a data center, operating or planned. Living near one barely moves your opinion in either direction. The people angriest about data centers are, overwhelmingly, people who have never lived near one.

This is just anger about AI and political strife. This issue will die once there are no politicians to pressure ahead of an election.

The cell phone towers that we used to hate ended up dressed up as pine trees in rural areas. Data centers have been built in the middle of downtown Manhattan, dressed as ordinary office buildings, and nobody complains. Industry will get better at putting floats in fall fairs, paying for schools and hospitals and rec centers, and integrating architectural improvements that make it feel harmonious with communities.

The movement against data centers on Facebook is already showing this slowdown. The 580 local opposition groups holding 640,000 Facebook memberships are not increasing at the same rate that they used to. I think this probably represents less than 400,000 people total and 18% of this entire national total sits inside a single group in Missouri.

These will not last. There are bigger and better ways to hate AI than something that brings wealth and success to rural communities that have been disenfranchised and ignored for 25 years.

playing with real money

Augusta Township in Michigan voted rezoning down at 89%: 2,583 votes. All told, the movement counts $130 billion of projects as blocked or delayed. There’s just no way that with all of this happening we cannot find a way forward; inference is simply too good a business.

I was really impressed by a recent Dwarkesh podcast featuring Dylan from SemiAnalysis and their discussion around just how valuable data centers are. We will inevitably find a way to fix this.

kooky cell phone tower ‘revolt’

In the 90s America convinced itself that cell towers were a public health emergency. Zoning calendars filled up with testimony about tumors and the fights were sincere across the country; people genuinely believed that these towers were making them sick.

Today those panics are barely remembered at all: a conspiracy theory from the fax machine era. Congress, in the 1996 Telecom Act, barred local governments from blocking towers over radio frequency health fears as long as the equipment met federal limits.

The reason why people stopped complaining about cell phone towers is because phones became indispensable. It took us a little while to get there. We didn’t have a great mobile phone even at the end of the 90s, but we got there. You could not pull smartphones out of America today if you tried, and the same exact thing will happen with AI.

A gigawatt campus is a bigger neighbour than a monopole; harder to shoehorn into a rural community. That’s what the money is for. The only difference between these two groups, pragmatically speaking, is that telecom has always been good about telling a story of the importance of their build-out, even as they genuinely ignored rural communities. How long have you been having a fight about rural broadband in the United States? The building trades told The Wall Street Journal that they will oppose candidates who attack data centers and the IBEW alone is 900,000 members.

a factory with no smokestack

We’ve spent forty years begging heavy industry to come home to America. Facility against facility, the largest hyperscale campus in the country emits roughly one hundredth of the smog-forming NOx of one Indiana steel mill and around one-thousandth of the fine particulates, two to three orders of magnitude cleaner, building for building. If you add up the entire national data center fleet in the EPA’s inventory, one single mill still out-emits all of it, 5.9 times over on NOx and 47 times over on fine particulates. One cement plant in Alpena, Michigan, beats the whole fleet on NOx by itself.

No facility classified as a data center has ever emitted enough on-site to trigger EPA’s greenhouse gas reporting floor. A data center supports far fewer permanent jobs per megawatt than conventional industrial projects but it also produces demonstrably less of the negative externalities that poison rural communities. Loudoun County’s own accounting says a dollar of services provided to data centers returns 26 dollars of tax revenue, against a manufacturing norm that rarely beats four. On the jobs math a data center is much like a chip fab and no one’s calling TSMC Arizona a jobs failure.
